title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
description:
A trie (pronounced as "try") or prefix tree is a tree data structure used to efficiently store and retrieve keys in a dataset of strings. It supports fast prefix-based lookups for applications such as autocomplete and spellcheckers.

Implement the `Trie` class:
- `Trie()` initializes the trie object.
- `void insert(String word)` inserts the string `word` into the trie.
- `boolean search(String word)` returns `true` if the exact string `word` is in the trie (i.e., was previously inserted), and `false` otherwise.
- `boolean startsWith(String prefix)` returns `true` if there is any previously inserted string in the trie that has the prefix `prefix`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: 1 <= word.length, prefix.length <= 2000
word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls in total will be made to insert, search, and startsWith.
hints: Represent each node with a map or fixed 26-element array of child links indexed by character, plus a boolean flag indicating whether a complete word ends at that node.
To insert a word, walk from the root creating missing child nodes for each character, and mark the final node as a word boundary.

Both search and startsWith traverse the trie character by character; startsWith returns true as soon as all prefix characters exist, while search also requires the final node's word-end flag to be true.

examples.explanation: After inserting "apple", searching "apple" returns true, searching "app" returns false (it is only a prefix so far), and startsWith("app") returns true. After inserting "app", searching "app" returns true.
With "cat", "car", and "dog" inserted, "ca" is a valid prefix but not a complete word, "car" is found, "do" is a valid prefix, and "bat" matches no inserted word's prefix.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
description:
Design a data structure that supports adding new words and finding if a string matches any previously added string.

Implement the `WordDictionary` class:
- `WordDictionary()` initializes the object.
- `void addWord(String word)` adds `word` to the data structure so it can be matched later.
- `boolean search(String word)` returns `true` if there is any string in the data structure that matches `word`, or `false` otherwise. `word` may contain dots `'.'` where each dot can match any single lowercase English letter.
constraints: 1 <= word.length <= 25
word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters.
word in search consists of '.' or lowercase English letters.
There will be at most 3 dots in word for search queries.
At most 10^4 calls will be made to addWord and search.
hints: Store all added words in a trie so exact characters can be traversed in O(1) per character.
When search encounters a regular letter, follow the single matching child link; when it encounters '.', recursively try every existing child of the current node.
Return true only when the recursion reaches the end of the query string on a trie node marked as the end of a word.
timeComplexity: O(L) addWord, O(26^d * L) worst-case search

examples.explanation: After adding "bad", "dad", and "mad", "pad" is not found, "bad" matches exactly, ".ad" matches any of the three words, and "b.." matches "bad".
With "a" and "ab" added, "." matches "a", ".." matches "ab", "..." matches no word of length 3, and both "a." and ".b" match "ab".

title: Word Search II
description:
Given an `m x n` grid of characters `board` and an array of unique strings `words`, return all words from `words` that can be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells on the board.

Adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. The same cell may not be used more than once in a single word. You may return the found words in any order, without duplicates.
constraints: m == board.length
n == board[i].length
board[i][j] is a lowercase English letter.
1 <= words.length <= 3 * 10^4
1 <= words[i].length <= 10
words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
All strings in words are unique.
hints: Searching each word independently repeats huge amounts of backtracking work. Insert all candidate words into a trie first.
Run DFS from every cell on the board, advancing through the board and the trie simultaneously so branches that match no prefix are pruned immediately.

Mark cells temporarily as visited during DFS and restore them on backtrack. Clear a trie node's stored word once found (and optionally prune empty leaf nodes) to avoid duplicate results and speed up later searches.

examples.explanation: Both "oath" ((0,0) -> (0,1) -> (1,1) -> (2,1)) and "eat" ((1,3) -> (1,2) -> (1,1)) exist on the board, while "pea" and "rain" do not.
No valid horizontally or vertically adjacent path spells "abcb" without reusing cells.

title: Replace Words
description:
In English, we have a concept called **root**, which can be followed by some other word to form another longer word called a **derivative**. For example, when the root `"help"` is followed by `"ful"`, we can form the derivative `"helpful"`.

Given a `dictionary` consisting of many roots and a `sentence` consisting of words separated by single spaces, replace all derivatives in the sentence with the root forming it. If a derivative can be replaced by more than one root, replace it with the root that has the **shortest length**.

Return the resulting sentence after the replacements.
constraints: 1 <= dictionary.length <= 1000
1 <= dictionary[i].length <= 100
dictionary[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.
1 <= sentence.length <= 10^6
sentence consists of only lowercase English letters and spaces.
The number of words in sentence is in the range [1, 1000].
The length of each word in sentence is in the range [1, 1000].
Every two consecutive words in sentence are separated by a single space.
sentence does not have leading or trailing spaces.
hints: Insert all roots from the dictionary into a trie.
For each word in the sentence, walk down the trie character by character from the root.
Stop immediately at the first trie node marked as a word end — that guarantees you select the shortest matching root. If you fall off the trie without hitting a word end, keep the original word.

examples.input: dictionary = ["cat","bat","rat"], sentence = "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
examples.output: "the cat was rat by the bat"
examples.explanation: "cattle" is replaced by "cat", "rattled" by "rat", and "battery" by "bat"; all other words have no matching root.
Every word begins with one of the single-letter roots "a", "b", or "c", so each word is replaced by its first letter.

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return the maximum result of `nums[i] XOR nums[j]`, where `0 <= i <= j < nums.length`.

Note that `i` and `j` may be equal (in which case `nums[i] XOR nums[i] = 0`).
constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 2 * 10^5
hints: To maximize the XOR of two numbers, you want their binary representations to differ in the highest possible bit positions.
Insert the 31-bit binary representation of each number (from bit 30 down to bit 0) into a binary trie.
For each number, traverse the trie from the most significant bit to the least significant bit, greedily choosing the opposite bit branch whenever it exists.

examples.explanation: The maximum XOR is achieved by 5 XOR 25 = 28.
The maximum XOR is achieved by 91 XOR 36 = 127 (1011011 XOR 0100100 = 1111111 in binary).

title: Map Sum Pairs
description:
Design a map that allows you to map string keys to integer values and return the sum of the values whose keys have a given prefix.

Implement the `MapSum` class:
- `MapSum()` initializes the `MapSum` object.
- `void insert(String key, int val)` inserts the `key-val` pair into the map. If `key` already existed, the original key-value pair is overridden with the new value.
- `int sum(String prefix)` returns the sum of all the pairs' values whose key starts with `prefix`. If no key starts with `prefix`, return `0`.
constraints: 1 <= key.length, prefix.length <= 50
key and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters.
At most 1000 calls will be made to insert and sum.
hints: Store a running prefix sum at every node of a trie so sum(prefix) only needs to walk along the characters of prefix in O(L) time.
Because insert can overwrite an existing key, also maintain a hash map recording each key's latest value.
On insert(key, val), compute delta = val - oldVal (with oldVal = 0 if new), update the map, and add delta to every trie node along key.

examples.explanation: After inserting ("apple", 3), sum("ap") is 3. After inserting ("app", 2), both "apple" and "app" start with "ap", giving 3 + 2 = 5.
Overwriting "apple" from 3 to 5 updates the prefix sum for "ap" from 5 to 7, while sum("apple") returns 5.

title: Concatenated Words
description:
Given an array of unique strings `words`, return all the **concatenated words** in the given list.

A **concatenated word** is defined as a string that is comprised entirely of at least two shorter words (not necessarily distinct) from the given array. You may return the answer in any order.
constraints: 1 <= words.length <= 10^4
1 <= words[i].length <= 30
words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.
All strings in words are unique.
1 <= sum(words[i].length) <= 10^5
hints: Sort words in ascending order of length so that any shorter words that could form a concatenated word have already been processed.

Store previously seen base words in a trie. For each candidate word, run DFS or DP with memoization walking the trie from each starting index to test whether the word can be segmented using words currently in the trie.

Because words are distinct and sorted by length, any full segmentation using existing trie words automatically uses at least two words — and concatenated words do not even need to be inserted into the trie.

examples.explanation: "catsdogcats" = "cats" + "dog" + "cats", "dogcatsdog" = "dog" + "cats" + "dog", and "ratcatdogcat" = "rat" + "cat" + "dog" + "cat".
"catdog" can be formed by concatenating "cat" and "dog".

title: Implement Magic Dictionary
description:
Design a data structure that is initialized with a list of distinct words. Provided a query string, you should determine if you can change **exactly one** character in this string to a different lowercase English letter so that it matches any string in the data structure.

Implement the `MagicDictionary` class:
- `MagicDictionary()` initializes the object.
- `void buildDict(String[] dictionary)` sets the data structure with an array of distinct strings `dictionary`.
- `boolean search(String searchWord)` returns `true` if you can change exactly one character in `searchWord` to match any string in the data structure, and `false` otherwise. Note that an exact match with zero changes does not count unless another dictionary word differs by exactly one character.
constraints: 1 <= dictionary.length <= 100
1 <= dictionary[i].length <= 100
dictionary[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.
All strings in dictionary are distinct.
1 <= searchWord.length <= 100
searchWord consists of only lowercase English letters.
buildDict is called once before search queries.
At most 100 calls will be made to search.
hints: Insert all dictionary words into a trie during buildDict.
For search(searchWord), run a DFS carrying the current character index, current trie node, and a boolean flag indicating whether the one allowed character modification has already been used.

If the modification has not been used yet, you may either follow the exact character (keeping modified = false) or follow any other existing child (setting modified = true). At the end of searchWord, return true only if modified is true and the node is a word end.
timeComplexity: O(N * L) buildDict, O(26 * L^2) worst-case search

examples.explanation: "hello" requires 0 changes so it returns false; "hhllo" can change the second 'h' to 'e' to match "hello" (true); "hell" and "leetcoded" have wrong lengths (false).
Because both "hello" and "hallo" are in the dictionary, searching "hello" now returns true (change 'e' to 'a' to match "hallo").

title: Stream of Characters
description:
Design an algorithm that accepts a stream of characters and checks whether any suffix of the characters queried so far forms a string from a given array of strings `words`.

For example, if `words = ["abc", "xyz"]` and the stream adds one by one `'a'`, `'x'`, `'y'`, `'z'`, your algorithm should detect that the suffix `"xyz"` of the queried characters `"axyz"` matches `"xyz"` from `words`.

Implement the `StreamChecker` class:
- `StreamChecker(String[] words)` initializes the object with the array `words`.
- `boolean query(char letter)` accepts a new character from the stream and returns `true` if any non-empty suffix from the stream forms a word in `words`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: 1 <= words.length <= 2000
1 <= words[i].length <= 200
words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
letter is a lowercase English letter.
At most 4 * 10^4 calls will be made to query.
hints: Checking suffixes of a growing stream is equivalent to checking prefixes of the reversed stream.
Insert every word in reversed order into a trie, and record the maximum word length L.
Keep only the last L queried characters in a buffer. On each query, walk backwards from the newest character through the reversed trie and return true as soon as you hit a word-end node.
timeComplexity: O(W * L) build, O(L) per query

examples.explanation: The stream receives a, b, c, d (matches "cd"), e, f (matches "f"), g, h, i, j, k, l (matches "kl").
As characters arrive, "aaab" matches on the 6th query, "ba" on the 7th, "ab" on the 8th, "ba" on the 9th, and "ab"/"abab" on the 10th.

title: Design In-Memory File System
description:
Design a data structure that simulates an in-memory file system.

Implement the `FileSystem` class:
- `FileSystem()` initializes the object of the system with an empty root directory `"/"`.
- `List<String> ls(String path)`:
  - If `path` is a file path, returns a list containing only this file's name.
  - If `path` is a directory path, returns the list of file and directory names directly inside this directory, sorted in **lexicographical order**.
- `void mkdir(String path)` creates a new directory at the given `path`. If middle directories in the path do not exist, create them as well.
- `void addContentToFile(String filePath, String content)`:
  - If `filePath` does not exist, creates that file containing `content`.
  - If `filePath` already exists, appends `content` to its existing content.
- `String readContentFromFile(String filePath)` returns the content of the file at `filePath`.
constraints: 1 <= path.length, filePath.length <= 100
path and filePath are absolute paths starting with '/' and do not end with '/' except when the path is '/' itself.
All directory and file names consist only of lowercase English letters, and no two entries in the same directory share the same name.
All operations are valid: ls is only called on existing paths, readContentFromFile is only called on existing files, and mkdir is never called on an existing file path.
1 <= content.length <= 50
At most 300 calls in total will be made to ls, mkdir, addContentToFile, and readContentFromFile.
hints: Model the directory hierarchy as a trie where each edge is a path segment (directory or file name) rather than a single character.
Each trie node stores a map from child name to child node, a boolean flag marking whether it is a file, and a string buffer holding its content if it is a file.
Using a sorted map (such as TreeMap in Java) or sorting child keys on ls ensures directory listings are always returned in lexicographical order.
timeComplexity: O(P + K log K) for ls, O(P + C) for file ops

examples.explanation: Initially "/" is empty. After mkdir("/a/b/c") and adding "hello" to "/a/b/c/d", ls("/") returns ["a"] and reading "/a/b/c/d" returns "hello".
ls("/") returns files and directories sorted lexicographically as ["a","m","z"]. Appending to "/m" concatenates the content, and ls("/m") returns only the file name ["m"].
